items.title: Gentrification displaces existing residents through rising rents
items.claim: What is the mechanism of gentrification?

options.text: A purely positive process with no losers

Wealthier newcomers move into a previously disinvested neighbourhood; property prices and rents rise; existing lower-income residents (often disproportionately ethnic minority) are displaced — Neil Smith's 'rent gap' theory (1979) explains the economic mechanism
State demolition of all old housing

items.reveal:
Ruth Glass coined 'gentrification' in 1964 in 'London: Aspects of Change', describing the takeover of Islington working-class housing by middle-class incomers. Neil Smith's 'rent gap' theory (1979) explained the economic incentive: the gap between actual rent under disinvestment and potential rent after re-investment attracts capital.

London examples: Notting Hill (1960s onwards), Brixton (2000s), Hackney (2000s-2010s). Berlin: Prenzlauer Berg, Kreuzberg. New York: SoHo, Williamsburg.

Mitigation policies — affordable housing quotas, right-to-return clauses on estate redevelopment, rent control — have variable effectiveness. Sharon Zukin and others have argued the cultural displacement (loss of community) is as significant as the housing displacement.
items.why: Urban regeneration produces winners and losers. 'Rejuvenation' narratives obscure who is being displaced and who the city is being improved for — central to contemporary urban geography.

items.title: OS contour lines show points of equal elevation
items.claim: What do OS contour lines show?

options.text: Lines connecting points of equal elevation above sea level — close contours indicate steep slopes; OS 1:50,000 Landranger maps typically use 10 m intervals; 1:25,000 Explorer maps use 5 or 10 m intervals depending on relief

items.reveal:
Closed loop contours with highest values inside indicate a hill summit. V-shaped contours pointing uphill indicate river valleys (water flows perpendicular to contours, downhill). Cliffs are shown by hachures or special vertical symbols.

Index contours (heavier lines) are labelled — typically every 50 m on 1:50,000 maps. Spot heights and trig points (triangulation pillars) give precise local elevations.

OS symbol conventions: black for human features, blue for water, brown for relief, green for vegetation, purple for tourist information. Knowing the key is half the skill.
items.why: Map literacy is portable across navigation, fieldwork and planning. Visual grammar (contour interval, symbol conventions) underpins all higher-level interpretation.

items.title: An aftershock larger than the mainshock becomes the new mainshock
items.claim: What is the relationship between mainshocks and aftershocks?

options.text: Aftershocks are always at least one magnitude smaller

If a later quake in the sequence is larger, it is retrospectively called the mainshock and the earlier event becomes a foreshock — so by definition the named mainshock is the largest; aftershocks typically follow Båth's law (around 1.2 magnitudes smaller) and Omori's law (rate decays as 1/t)
Aftershocks are unrelated to the mainshock

items.reveal:
Båth's law (1965) gives the largest aftershock as typically about 1.2 magnitudes smaller than the mainshock. Omori's law (1894) describes the rate decay: aftershocks fall off as 1/t after the main event.

The 2011 Christchurch earthquake (M6.3, 22 February 2011) was an aftershock of the September 2010 Darfield earthquake (M7.1). Because it was smaller, it kept the aftershock label — but it killed 185 people because it was shallower, closer to the city centre, and hit during business hours.

Aftershock sequences can continue for years after large events — the New Madrid 1811-12 sequence still produces detectable aftershocks two centuries later.
items.why: Statistical naming hides hazard. A 'smaller' aftershock can do more damage than its mainshock if its location and depth are worse — Christchurch is the canonical case.
